Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] UniFi OS CVE-2026-34908/34909 auth bypass via /api/auth/validate-sso/ URI normalization · [LLM] UniFi OS CVE-2026-34910 command injection via ucs/update/latest_package endpoint
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Anomalous child processes spawned under UniFi ucs-update service (post-exploitation)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

Hunts for unauthenticated requests to the UniFi OS Server that contain the auth-exempt prefix /api/auth/validate-sso/ but resolve (post-normalization) to protected backend routes. Bishop Fox confirmed this URI mismatch is the entry point of the unauth RCE chain on UniFi OS Server <= 5.0.6. Rationale: Anchors on the article's two named strings: the auth-exempt prefix '/api/auth/validate-sso/' and the protected target endpoint 'ucs/update/latest_package'. Combined with traversal / semicolon-based URI normalization artifacts (the documented root cause is a normalization mismatch between the auth filter and Nginx), the combination is high-fidelity. Cross-checked with the Bishop Fox advisory referenced in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://bishopfox.com/blog/cve-2026-34908-34909-34910-ubiquiti-unifi-os-rce • https://community.ui.com/releases/UniFi-OS-Server-5-0-8/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
// UniFi appliances typically aren't onboarded to MDE; this query catches Defender-protected Windows reverse proxies fronting UniFi.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (443, 8443, 11443)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" or LocalIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("nginx.exe","haproxy.exe","caddy.exe","iisexpress.exe","w3wp.exe")
| where AdditionalFields has "/api/auth/validate-sso/"
| where AdditionalFields has_any ("../","%2e%2e%2f","%2e%2e/","..%2f","ucs/update/latest_package",";","%3b")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
// Path A — Syslog from the UniFi appliance itself (nginx access log shipped via rsyslog)
let validate_sso_abuse = Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName in~ ("nginx","unifi-os","ucs")
| where SyslogMessage has "/api/auth/validate-sso/"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("../","%2e%2e%2f","%2e%2e/","..%2f","ucs/update/latest_package",";","%3b")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage;
// Path B — WAF / NGFW logs in CommonSecurityLog (DeviceName lives elsewhere; CSL uses DeviceVendor + DestinationHostName)
let validate_sso_csl = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort in (443, 8443, 11443)
| where RequestURL has "/api/auth/validate-sso/"
| where RequestURL has_any ("../","%2e%2e%2f","%2e%2e/","..%2f","ucs/update/latest_package",";","%3b")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication;
union validate_sso_abuse, validate_sso_csl
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] UniFi OS CVE-2026-34910 command injection via ucs/update/latest_package endpoint Exploitation High
Hunts for direct requests to the package-update endpoint 'ucs/update/latest_package' that carry shell-metacharacter payloads in the body or query string. Per Bishop Fox, this is the command-injection sink at the end of the chain — unvalidated user input is concatenated into a shell command executed by the ucs-update service account. Rationale: Direct lift of the two strings the article explicitly tells defenders to monitor ('ucs/update/latest_package' and the package-update injection sink), combined with the canonical Unix shell metacharacter set ( ; | ` $() && || newline & ) and their URL-encoded equivalents. Any legitimate UniFi update will not include shell metachars in the URI. Cross-checked Bishop Fox write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://bishopfox.com/blog/cve-2026-34908-34909-34910-ubiquiti-unifi-os-rce

[LLM] Anomalous child processes spawned under UniFi ucs-update service (post-exploitation) Installation High
Hunts on UniFi OS appliances (Linux) for unexpected child processes of the ucs-update service binary — the post-injection foothold described by Bishop Fox. Legitimate ucs-update only invokes the package manager and a small set of UniFi helper binaries; spawn of bash/sh/curl/wget/nc/python is high-confidence post-exploitation. Rationale: Bishop Fox's recommended hunting hint is verbatim: 'suspicious child processes under ucs-update'. The ucs-update binary in normal operation only invokes the package manager and a couple of UniFi helper utilities — any interpreter, network tool, or sudo invocation downstream of it is post-exploitation. Also covers the sudo→root escalation step the article calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://bishopfox.com/blog/cve-2026-34908-34909-34910-ubiquiti-unifi-os-rce • https://community.ui.com/releases/UniFi-OS-Server-5-0-8/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1068 T1548.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
// Requires Defender for Endpoint on Linux on the UniFi appliance (or a Linux jump host running ucs-update tooling)
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ucs-update","ucs","unifi-os")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php","sudo","chmod","chown","base64","openssl","ssh","scp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
// Path A — auditd/syslog from the appliance
let ucs_children_syslog = Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility in~ ("auth","authpriv","daemon","user")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("ucs-update","unifi-os")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/bin/bash","/bin/sh","/usr/bin/curl","/usr/bin/wget","/bin/nc","/usr/bin/socat","/usr/bin/python","/usr/bin/perl","sudo ","chmod ","base64 -d","openssl enc")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage;
// Path B — ASIM process create (cross-vendor portable)
let ucs_children_asim = ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ucs-update","ucs","unifi-os")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php","sudo","chmod","chown","base64","openssl","ssh","scp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine;
union ucs_children_syslog, ucs_children_asim
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI Phishing Is Crushing SOCs with Alert Volume: How to Reduce Tier 1 Overload

The Hacker News
2026-06-08 7 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Phishing has always been a numbers game. AI has turned it into a volume machine. Attackers can now create convincing emails, fake login pages, and tailored lures in minutes. Every polished message adds another case for Tier 1 to review, another link to inspect, and another alert that cannot be dismissed at a glance. As the queue grows, a credential theft attempt or malware delivery can easily

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ⚡ Weekly Recap: Instagram Account Hacks, Android Zero-Day, GitHub Worm and More
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental

| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound IKEv1 traffic from Qilin VPN-bypass infrastructure to Check Point gateways
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Check Point IKEv1 Remote Access VPN session with no machine certificate (CVE-2026-50751 bypass shape)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Qilin post-compromise payload hashes (52fda5c1, 51d39aa3) on hosts reachable from VPN concentrator · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Long-lived VPN tunnel from VPS hosting ranges (Vultr/Cogent) attributed to Qilin VPN-bypass C2 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Inbound IKEv1 traffic from Qilin VPN-bypass infrastructure to Check Point gateways Delivery High
Hunts for inbound IKE/IPsec traffic (UDP/500, UDP/4500, ESP) sourced from the eight IP addresses attributed to the CVE-2026-50751 exploitation campaign against Check Point Remote Access / Mobile Access / Spark / Security Gateway products. Any successful association from these IPs against a Check Point firewall is a high-confidence indicator of the Qilin-affiliated VPN auth bypass. Rationale: Uses the eight attacker IPs from Phase 1/3 of the kill-chain (article-confirmed). Pairs them with IKE/IPsec ports (UDP 500/4500/ESP) so the detection fires only on VPN-shape traffic, not generic web noise. Cross-checked against: • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk183303
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167")
| where RemotePort in (500, 4500) or Protocol =~ "esp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let QilinIPs = dynamic(["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Check Point"
| where SourceIP in (QilinIPs)
| where DestinationPort in (500, 4500) or ApplicationProtocol in~ ("ike","isakmp","esp","ipsec")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, DeviceAction, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DestinationHostName, ApplicationProtocol, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 5e9b1a6b-2f7d-4d4d-89c9-1ef6ad8d4321
description: Detects inbound IKE/IPsec packets originating from IP addresses attributed to the Qilin-affiliated exploitation of CVE-2026-50751 against Check Point Remote Access VPN gateways.
references:

date: 2026/06/08
tags:

  - attack.t1133
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: firewall
detection:

  condition: selection
level: high
source:(windows.defender OR cloudtrail OR azure.activity_logs OR linux.syslog) (@network.client.ip:45.77.149.152 OR @network.client.ip:209.182.225.136 OR @network.client.ip:38.60.157.139 OR @network.client.ip:162.33.177.101 OR @network.client.ip:45.76.26.42 OR @network.client.ip:144.208.127.155 OR @network.client.ip:38.54.88.201 OR @network.client.ip:38.54.107.167)
(#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6)
| in(field=RemoteAddressIP4, values=["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"])

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as dest_ip values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port values(All_Traffic.transport) as transport from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_ip IN ("45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167") AND (All_Traffic.dest_port IN (500,4500) OR All_Traffic.transport="esp") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as dest_ip values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port values(All_Traffic.transport) as transport from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_ip IN ("45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167") AND (All_Traffic.dest_port IN (500,4500) OR All_Traffic.transport="esp") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
[LLM] Check Point IKEv1 Remote Access VPN session with no machine certificate (CVE-2026-50751 bypass shape) Exploitation High
Hunts for successful Remote Access / Mobile Access VPN authentications that negotiated over IKEv1 without a machine certificate — the exact configuration the CVE-2026-50751 auth bypass targets. Surfaces gateways still accepting legacy RA clients that need to be hardened, and any session that successfully authenticated via the vulnerable path during the May 7 onwards exploitation window. Rationale: Targets the exact misconfiguration the article calls out: IKEv1 + legacy RA client + no mandatory machine certificate. Fires on the vulnerable shape regardless of source IP, so it catches exploitation from IPs not yet on the IOC list. Cross-checked Check Point advisory sk183303 wording. Cross-checked against: • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk183303 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/
ATT&CKT1190 T1556 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
// Downstream view — endpoints authenticating to AD via Check Point VPN pool, no Defender direct visibility of the IKE handshake itself
let VpnAttackerSrc = dynamic(["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"]);
IdentityLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(45d)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where Protocol in~ ("Kerberos","NTLM","Ldap")
| where IPAddress in (VpnAttackerSrc)
   or DeviceName has_any ("vpn","ra-","mobileaccess","checkpoint")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountUpn, AccountName, IPAddress, DeviceName, Protocol, LogonType, Application
| order by Timestamp desc
let QilinIPs = dynamic(["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Check Point"
| where Activity has_any ("Log In","Authentication","VPN Successful","Key Install","IKE")
| where DeviceCustomString1 has "IKEv1" or DeviceCustomString2 has "IKEv1" or Message has "IKEv1" or AdditionalExtensions has "IKEv1"
| where not(Message has_any ("machine_certificate","machine certificate","cert_auth")) and not(AdditionalExtensions has_any ("machine_certificate","machine certificate"))
| extend HitsAttackerIP = iff(SourceIP in (QilinIPs), "YES", "no")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, DeviceAction, SourceUserName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, ApplicationProtocol, HitsAttackerIP, Message
| order by HitsAttackerIP desc, TimeGenerated desc
source:checkpoint (@evt.name:("Log In" OR Authentication OR "VPN Successful" OR "Key Install")) AND (@ike.version:1 OR @message:IKEv1) AND -@auth.method:(machine_certificate OR cert)

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.user) as user values(Authentication.src) as src_ip values(Authentication.dest) as gateway from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("checkpoint","checkpoint-fw","checkpoint-mobileaccess","checkpoint-ra") AND Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.signature Authentication.authentication_method Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | search authentication_method="IKEv1" OR signature="*legacy*" OR signature="*ike_v1*" | search NOT authentication_method IN ("machine_certificate","cert","x509") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.user) as user values(Authentication.src) as src_ip values(Authentication.dest) as gateway from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("checkpoint","checkpoint-fw","checkpoint-mobileaccess","checkpoint-ra") AND Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.signature Authentication.authentication_method Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | search authentication_method="IKEv1" OR signature="*legacy*" OR signature="*ike_v1*" | search NOT authentication_method IN ("machine_certificate","cert","x509") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
[LLM] Long-lived VPN tunnel from VPS hosting ranges (Vultr/Cogent) attributed to Qilin VPN-bypass C2 Command & Control Medium
Hunts for inbound VPN sessions that stay open for hours from the eight Qilin-attributed IPs, plus any east-west traffic from the VPN-pool address those sessions were assigned. Models the article's described C2 pattern: attacker holds an interactive remote-access tunnel for hands-on-keyboard activity, traffic appears to originate from a trusted RA-VPN IP. Rationale: Pivots on the Phase 3 C2 hint that several attacker IPs sit in Vultr / Cogent VPS ranges and the tunnels are long-lived for hands-on-keyboard activity. Combines IP IOCs with a duration threshold so a one-off probe is filtered out — only sustained sessions surface. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/check-point-links-vpn-zero-day-attacks-to-qilin-ransomware-gang/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
let QilinIPs = dynamic(["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (QilinIPs) or LocalIP in (QilinIPs)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Bytes=sum(toint(coalesce(tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).BytesSent),"0"))) by DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName
| extend DurationMin = datetime_diff("minute", LastSeen, FirstSeen)

[LLM] Qilin post-compromise payload hashes (52fda5c1, 51d39aa3) on hosts reachable from VPN concentrator Installation High
Alerts on execution, file write, or image load of the two MD5 hashes attributed to the post-exploitation activity of the Qilin ransomware affiliate after CVE-2026-50751 was exploited. Highest-fidelity signal in the chain — anywhere these hashes appear on an internal host is a confirmed Qilin landing. Rationale: Both hashes are Phase 2/4 IOCs attributed to the confirmed Qilin post-compromise activity in the article and the kill-chain block. Hash hits are deterministic — no rephrasing needed; any match anywhere on the estate is high-severity. Sentinel union covers ASIM, SecurityEvent 4688 and CommonSecurityLog so detection works whether the customer uses MDE, Sysmon, or a third-party EDR shipping to CEF. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/check-point-links-vpn-zero-day-attacks-to-qilin-ransomware-gang/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1032/
ATT&CKT1486 T1657 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let QilinHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689","51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
   | where MD5 in (QilinHashes) or InitiatingProcessMD5 in (QilinHashes)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, EventTable="DeviceProcessEvents", FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
   | where MD5 in (QilinHashes)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, EventTable="DeviceFileEvents", FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine="", AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
   | where MD5 in (QilinHashes)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, EventTable="DeviceImageLoadEvents", FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine="", AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine="")
| order by Timestamp desc
let QilinHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689","51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
   | where MD5 in (QilinHashes) or Hash in (QilinHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, EventTable="ImProcessCreate", Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, FileName=ActingProcessName, FilePath="", MD5, SHA256, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentImage=ParentProcessName, ParentCommandLine=ParentProcessCommandLine),
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
   | where TargetFileMD5 in (QilinHashes) or Hash in (QilinHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, EventTable="ImFileEvent", Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, FileName=TargetFileName, FilePath=TargetFilePath, MD5=TargetFileMD5, SHA256=TargetFileSHA256, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentImage=ActingProcessName, ParentCommandLine=""),
  (SecurityEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
   | where EventID == 4688
   | where FileHash has_any (QilinHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, EventTable="SecurityEvent4688", Host=Computer, ActorUsername=SubjectUserName, FileName=NewProcessName, FilePath=NewProcessName, MD5=FileHash, SHA256="", CommandLine, ParentImage=ParentProcessName, ParentCommandLine=""),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
   | where FileHash in~ (QilinHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, EventTable="CommonSecurityLog", Host=coalesce(SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, DeviceName), ActorUsername=SourceUserName, FileName, FilePath, MD5=FileHash, SHA256="", CommandLine="", ParentImage=ProcessName, ParentCommandLine="")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50751", "CVE-2026-50752")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50751", "CVE-2026-50752")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VerdantBamboo Deploys BSD Variant of BRICKSTORM on Linux Appliances

The Hacker News
2026-06-08 14 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A China-nexus cyber espionage group has been observed deploying a BSD variant of a known backdoor called BRICKSTORM, as well as two other malware families codenamed PLENET (aka GRIMBOLT) and AGENTPSD to target Linux systems. The activity has been attributed by Volexity to a threat cluster it tracks as VerdantBamboo, which it said overlaps with hacking groups known as Clay Typhoon (Microsoft),

[LLM] M365 / Entra sign-ins sourced from BRICKSTORM C2 IP 149.248.11.71 Command & Control High
Hunts Microsoft 365 / Entra ID sign-in events whose source IP matches the VerdantBamboo C2 address published by Volexity. Because the actor proxied through compromised Egnyte Storage Sync + pfSense BRICKSTORM SOCKS relays to blend into Conditional Access policies, any direct sign-in from this IP indicates either a misconfigured tunnel or direct actor probing. Rationale: 149.248.11.71 is the sole IP IOC published by Volexity and reposted by Bleeping Computer / Cybersecuritynews — high-fidelity point IOC. Cross-checked Volexity report and Mallory.ai write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-apt-deploys-new-malware-to-keep-access-to-hacked-networks/ • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019e9476-afd4-71fe-a6f0-7dff94b7f250

[LLM] VerdantBamboo BRICKSTORM / PLENET / AGENTPSD file-hash IOCs Installation High
Point-detection on the eight SHA256, four SHA1 and four MD5 hashes Volexity published for the BSD BRICKSTORM variant, PLENET (.NET AOT) and AGENTPSD (Python reverse shell). Matches across DeviceFileEvents and DeviceProcessEvents so we catch both landing and execution attempts on any Defender-for-Linux / Windows host. Rationale: All 16 hashes published in Volexity's June 2026 Verdant Bamboo blog; cross-checked against the BleepingComputer reposting of the IOC list. Hash detections have negligible FP rate; the broader IOC pivot covers the three malware families (BRICKSTORM BSD, PLENET, AGENTPSD) listed in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-apt-deploys-new-malware-to-keep-access-to-hacked-networks/ • https://github.com/mandiant/brickstorm-scanner

[LLM] AGENTPSD-style Python reverse shell spawned by sshd on Linux / NAS Installation Medium
Hunts the AGENTPSD deployment pattern Volexity describes: VerdantBamboo SSHed into Synology NAS / Linux appliances and dropped a Python-based reverse shell. Surfaces python3 / python processes whose parent is sshd and which subsequently open an outbound socket — a behaviour pattern that survives even when the static hashes mutate. Rationale: The article specifically calls out AGENTPSD as a Python reverse shell deployed over SSH to the Synology NAS. Parent=sshd + child=python is a tight behavioural pair on appliances where Python is rarely launched interactively; the cmd-line tokens are the canonical Python reverse-shell idioms. Cross-checked Volexity blog for the deployment vector (SSH). Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/chinese-apt-verdantbamboo-uses-brickstorm-malware/

| where FileName in~ ("python","python2","python3")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

[LLM] Outbound endpoint connections to BRICKSTORM C2 IP 149.248.11.71 Command & Control High
Catches any endpoint, server or appliance making an outbound network connection to the VerdantBamboo BRICKSTORM C2 address. Distinct pivot from UC1 (M365 sign-ins) — this targets the BRICKSTORM SOCKS callback channel rather than the resulting Entra session, so it fires even if the proxy never reaches a successful sign-in. Rationale: 149.248.11.71 is the only network-layer IOC Volexity published. The detection covers every host that BRICKSTORM might call out from (Storage Sync, pfSense, Synology NAS, Windows endpoints) by hitting both EDR and firewall telemetry. Cross-checked Volexity, BleepingComputer and Mallory.ai. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-apt-deploys-new-malware-to-keep-access-to-hacked-networks/

| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] pfSense / firewall config change enabling Web SSL VPN after admin login Installation Medium
Hunts the VerdantBamboo re-entry tactic Volexity documents — after stolen admin credentials let them into the firewall, the actor enabled web SSL VPN access to the appliance and used it for ongoing entry. Surfaces config-write events on the firewall WebGUI / SSL VPN service originating from previously-unseen admin source IPs, correlated to a successful admin login in the preceding 15 minutes. Rationale: Volexity explicitly describes the actor reconnecting to the firewall with stolen admin credentials and then enabling web SSL VPN access on the device — Syslog/php-fpm/configd messages on pfSense are the canonical witness for that change. Defender / Falcon are left empty because pfSense appliances are not typically EDR-instrumented; Sigma is left empty because the correlation requires a time-window join between two log events (rule explicitly forbidden for single-event-shape Sigma). Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/06/04/verdantbamboo-just-another-brickstorm-in-the-firewall/ • https://cyberpress.org/verdantbamboo-breaches-pfsense-firewall/

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
